title: Texas v. United States
lead: The states seek to stop a deferred-action program before implementation. A preliminary-injunction appeal turns on license costs, the difference between nonenforcement and benefits eligibility, and a disputed prediction of how agency discretion would operate.

actors.name: Texas and the plaintiff states
actors.role: Challenged the 2014 deferred-action memorandum; Texas relied on anticipated subsidized-license costs.

actors.name: Jeh Johnson
actors.role: Secretary of Homeland Security who issued the November 2014 memorandum.

actors.name: Department of Homeland Security and United States
actors.role: Defended the program and appealed the preliminary injunction.

actors.name: Kenneth Palinkas and Donald Neufeld
actors.role: Union president and USCIS official whose competing declarations informed the practical-discretion dispute.

proceedings: The district court entered a nationwide preliminary injunction on the procedural APA claim.
An earlier Fifth Circuit panel denied a stay at 787 F.3d 733.
The November 9, 2015 merits panel, revised November 25, affirmed two to one, adding statutory authority as an alternative ground.
limits: This narrative concerns the historical November 2015 preliminary-injunction appeal, not final trial relief or present immigration law. Original 2012 DACA was not enjoined. DAPA in this opinion includes the parental program and three 2014 DACA expansions. The Take Care claim and genuine individual deferred-action authority were not decided. Predictions and disputed evidence remain attributed.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: The Secretary expands deferred action in 2014
sections.cue: What changed, and what did the memorandum say recipients would receive?
paragraphs: The Department of Homeland Security’s 2012 Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, DACA, permitted qualifying people brought to the United States as children to request deferred action. It contemplated individual discretion and created neither citizenship nor an enforceable right to remain. In November 2014 Secretary Jeh Johnson issued a memorandum expanding DACA and creating Deferred Action for Parents of Americans and Lawful Permanent Residents, DAPA.

The opinion uses DAPA to include the parental program and three DACA changes: eliminating the age cap, extending deferred action from two years to three, and moving the arrival cutoff to January 1, 2010. Original 2012 DACA was outside the injunction. The parental program potentially covered about 4.3 million people. Applicants needed a citizen or lawful-permanent-resident child, continuous residence since before January 1, 2010, presence at specified times, no lawful status, no applicable enforcement priority, and no other factor making relief inappropriate in the officer’s discretion. They would provide biometrics and pay biometrics and work-authorization fees.

The memorandum repeatedly preserved individualized, revocable discretion and disclaimed substantive rights, immigration status or citizenship eligibility. Deferred action allowed lawful presence for specified purposes while leaving recipients removable. Existing statutes and regulations also permitted applications for work authorization and, if other conditions were satisfied, Social Security numbers and certain benefits. Eligibility did not automatically award every benefit. Whether these effects were affirmative DAPA action or consequences of otherwise unreviewable nonenforcement became a central disagreement.

sources.pinpoint: Facts and challenged program; slip 3–7, 35–40, 86–90; note 11; Appendix A

sections.title: The states obtain preliminary relief on a procedural theory
sections.cue: What was decided before the Fifth Circuit’s merits appeal?
paragraphs: Texas and other states alleged violations of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), both procedural and substantive, and of the Constitution’s Take Care Clause. The district court preliminarily enjoined the program nationwide for failure to use notice and comment, leaving the other claims unresolved. An earlier Fifth Circuit panel denied a stay; the present decision was the later merits appeal from the preliminary injunction, not that stay decision.

The appellate panel reviewed the injunction for abuse of discretion, findings for clear error and legal conclusions for correctness. The states needed substantial likelihood of success, threatened irreparable injury, a favorable balance of harms and consistency with the public interest. Judge Jerry E. Smith, joined by Judge Elrod, affirmed. Judge King dissented.

The majority also addressed substantive statutory authority as an independent ground, saying it was briefed and the parties agreed no more factual development was needed. It treated alternative holdings as circuit precedent. King thought the legal briefing insufficient and would avoid that question. Neither court decided the Take Care claim.

sources.pinpoint: Proceedings and review standard; slip 2 & n.3, 7–9, 54 & nn.157–158, 116–117

sections.title: Texas’s license costs establish standing for the majority
sections.cue: Why were those costs traceable and redressable despite state policy choices?
paragraphs: Texas presented anticipated costs of issuing subsidized driver’s licenses to newly eligible applicants: at least 500,000 potential beneficiaries and a loss of at least $130.89 per license. The majority treated extra tax or insurance benefits as distinct transactions rather than offsets to that particular expenditure. Texas had adopted its eligibility policy before DACA and DAPA, so the court did not regard the loss as manufactured for litigation. An option to raise fees or abandon an otherwise permissible policy did not defeat injury.

Relying on Massachusetts v. EPA’s treatment of state standing, the majority gave Texas special solicitude based on its APA procedural right and interest in its legal code within a federal immigration framework. It limited the analysis to these circumstances and did not decide whether excluding recipients from licenses would violate preemption or equal protection. Reconsideration after proper procedure was possible, and preventing implementation would prevent the identified costs. Other standing theories were unnecessary.

The states arguably fell within the Immigration and Nationality Act’s zone of interests, including provisions allowing withholding of specified benefits from unauthorized aliens. The government did not contest final agency action. Section 1252(g), dealing with specified removal decisions and claims by or for aliens, did not bar the states’ own program challenge.

sources.pinpoint: Texas’s standing and statutory reviewability; slip 9–34 & nn.46, 82

sections.title: The majority separates the program from ordinary enforcement priorities
sections.cue: What made review possible, and what evidence suggested a binding rule?
paragraphs: Under APA § 701(a)(2), ordinary nonenforcement is presumptively unreviewable. The majority instead characterized DAPA as an affirmative grant of lawful presence and associated eligibility. Detailed immigration and employment classifications provided legal standards. It did not decide whether the ordinary presumption could be rebutted because it found this program outside that category. The injunction required no removal and left separate enforcement priorities intact.

A policy statement leaves decisionmakers genuinely free; a substantive rule imposes rights or obligations through text or practical application. The majority recognized the memorandum’s discretionary language but relied on the district court’s prediction about implementation. DAPA would use procedures resembling DACA. Relevant evidence included DACA’s high approval rate, absence of quantified discretionary denials among otherwise qualified applicants, union president Kenneth Palinkas’s declaration, detailed operating and evidentiary directions, mandatory requests for evidence, implementation instructions and presidential compliance statements.

The majority acknowledged self-selection, different populations and DAPA’s added discretionary criteria. United States Citizenship and Immigration Services official Donald Neufeld described individualized review, evidence requests, interviews and discretionary denials. The majority nevertheless found no clear error: it regarded cited denial reasons as eligibility or enforcement criteria and emphasized missing counts distinguishing residual discretion. That was a contested inference, not an agreed fact that all eligible applications were always approved.

The district court had mistakenly called defective applications denials where the agency called them rejections. The majority thought the error nondecisive; King thought it central. The majority also emphasized that the government neither requested an evidentiary hearing nor claimed appellate error from its absence. King thought unresolved declarations demanded one. The source’s statement that the parental program had not been implemented cannot be expanded into no implementation of any 2014 DACA change; note 141 discussed disputed early activity.

sources.pinpoint: Reviewability; Notice and comment; Source scope; slip 34–50 & nn.108, 130, 133–142

sections.title: Procedural exceptions and statutory authority supply further disputes
sections.cue: Why would notice and comment alone not resolve the majority’s objections?
paragraphs: The majority rejected the procedural-rule exception because DAPA altered substantive interests under the Fifth Circuit’s substantial-impact approach and changed substantive benefit-evaluation standards under the D.C. Circuit’s different approach. It construed the public-benefits exception narrowly: collateral eligibility did not make an immigration program a benefit program managed by the issuing agency. The court did not thereby subject ordinary nonenforcement policy to notice and comment.

As an independent ground, the majority assumed without deciding that Chevron deference applied, then found Congress had directly addressed lawful presence and employment authorization through the Immigration and Nationality Act’s detailed structure. Family immigration routes, cancellation requirements and specified deferred-action categories did not authorize this broad parental program. The majority recognized that lawful presence differed from permanent residence but concluded that DAPA bypassed requirements linked to a child’s status.

General enforcement authority and the definitional reference to employment authorized by the Attorney General did not delegate a choice of this political and economic magnitude, in its view. Even if a gap remained, DAPA was manifestly contrary to the statutory scheme at Chevron’s second step. Earlier programs were limited, country-specific or bridges to statutory legalization. The majority reserved genuinely case-specific deferred action. Its statutory objection meant that completing notice and comment alone would not answer the decision.

sources.pinpoint: Notice and comment; Independent statutory-authority ground; Exam use; slip 50–66 & nn.146, 156, 160–174, 185–202

sections.title: King rejects the characterization, factual prediction and statutory conclusion
sections.cue: What alternative account supported dismissal or denial of the injunction?
paragraphs: Judge King would dismiss as nonjusticiable. She saw prosecutorial-discretion guidance, with collateral eligibility resulting from unchallenged preexisting statutes and notice-and-comment regulations. Revocable nonremoval did not become reviewable because other law attached consequences, and lawful presence was not immigration status. She also questioned standing from indirect costs Texas chose to bear and extension of Massachusetts’s special solicitude.

King considered the memorandum a policy statement requiring judgment through flexible priorities and an open-ended final criterion. Directing officers to exercise discretion did not remove it; detailed guidance could channel without fixing decisions. The parental program had no actual implementation record at the pertinent district-court stage, and DACA’s different criteria undermined the predictive analogy. Approval rates, selected statements, conflated rejections and denials, and transferring the injunction burden to the agency were inadequate. Neufeld’s declaration supported discretion and explained unavailable historical breakdowns; Palinkas’s conclusions and standardized forms did not prove mechanical administration. At minimum, King wanted a hearing on conflicting evidence.

King would avoid the statutory issue but also disagreed on its merits. Permanent-residence requirements did not precisely regulate revocable lawful presence; statutory recognition of some deferred-action categories did not prohibit other discretion. Practice, broad delegations and longstanding work-authorization regulations supported the agency. Immigration expertise distinguished the concern in King v. Burwell about assigning insurance policy to the Internal Revenue Service. Scale alone did not make permissible individual discretion unlawful.

The majority found irreparable losses because retracting licenses and benefits would be difficult, and found the balance and public interest favored the status quo. Uniform immigration administration and movement across state lines justified nationwide relief. On November 9, 2015, revised November 25, the court affirmed two to one. It ordered no deportations, granted no final trial relief, decided no Take Care violation, and did not invalidate all deferred action.

sources.pinpoint: King dissent; Injunction and judgment; slip 66–124 & dissent nn.13–31, 56–62
